findings.title: Reflected XSS in /salut/<nome> via unescaped f-string response
findings.accepted_input: URL path segment <nome> — no type constraint, any string accepted
findings.intended_control: route handler returns informational text to the caller
findings.crossed_boundary: attacker-controlled string embedded in HTML document delivered to victim browser
findings.affected_principal: any user tricked into clicking attacker-crafted URL
findings.observed_result: arbitrary HTML/JS from the URL path executes in victim's browser under the app origin

evidence.snippet: return f"Salut, {nume}! Bine ai venit în aplicația Flask."
evidence.note: Flask wraps bare string returns as text/html; charset=utf-8. No escaping or sanitization applied. All other templates use Jinja2 auto-escaping and are unaffected.

findings.fix: Use flask.escape(nume) or markupsafe.escape(nume), or return plain text via Response(text, mimetype='text/plain'). Simplest: `from markupsafe import escape; return f'Salut, {escape(nume)}!...'`

findings.title: Passwords stored and compared as plaintext — no hashing
findings.lower_trust_principal: attacker with database read access (file theft, backup exfiltration, or image inspection)
findings.crossed_boundary: storage layer → full credential set recovery with zero effort
findings.observed_result: every user's plaintext password readable directly from the users table

evidence.snippet: con.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO users (username, password) VALUES (?, ?)", ("admin", "admin123"))
con.execute("SELECT username FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?", (username, password))

findings.fix: Replace plaintext storage with bcrypt or argon2-cffi. Hash on registration/seed; verify with the library's check function. Example: `from bcrypt import hashpw, gensalt, checkpw`. Never store or compare the raw password string.

findings.title: Admin credentials hardcoded in source and displayed on public login page
findings.crossed_boundary: source code and unauthenticated page → admin credential disclosure
findings.affected_principal: admin account; any user whose credentials are seeded in source
findings.observed_result: admin/admin123 visible in app.py source and in the HTML of /login to any visitor; alina/alina123 and cosmin/cosmin123 also in source
findings.fix: Remove the hint from login.html. Seed admin and demo accounts from environment variables or a first-run script, never from hardcoded literals. With proper hashing (F-002 fix), seed a hashed value.

findings.title: Known fallback SECRET_KEY enables Flask session cookie forgery
findings.lower_trust_principal: attacker who knows the fallback key value
findings.accepted_input: HTTP request with a crafted session cookie signed with the known key
findings.intended_control: Flask session cookie is signed and tamper-evident
findings.crossed_boundary: attacker forges session cookie claiming any username → bypasses all authentication
findings.observed_result: if SECRET_KEY env var is absent at runtime, 'dev-only-secret-key' is used; flask-unsign or itsdangerous can forge a valid cookie with {"username": "admin"}
findings.fix: Remove the fallback literal. Raise a startup error if SECRET_KEY is absent or equals a known weak value. Require a minimum 32-byte random key. Example: `key = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]; assert len(key) >= 32`.

findings.title: FLASK_DEBUG=1 baked into production Dockerfile exposes Werkzeug interactive debugger
findings.lower_trust_principal: any user who can trigger a 500 error
findings.accepted_input: any HTTP request that causes an unhandled exception
findings.intended_control: production container serves the application without debug tooling
findings.crossed_boundary: unauthenticated user → arbitrary Python code execution inside the container via Werkzeug debug console
findings.affected_principal: entire container and any mounted secrets or volumes
findings.observed_result: debug mode enables the Werkzeug PIN-protected interactive debugger on 500 error pages; PIN is derivable from container filesystem data (documented in CVE-2019-14806 class)
findings.fix: Remove ENV FLASK_DEBUG=1 from the Dockerfile. Set FLASK_DEBUG only in a separate development override (e.g., docker-compose.override.yml) that is never deployed to production.

findings.title: SQLite database with plaintext credentials baked into Docker image
findings.lower_trust_principal: anyone who pulls or inspects the Docker image
findings.accepted_input: docker pull / docker image inspect / docker run
findings.crossed_boundary: image layer inspection → full plaintext credential dump
findings.observed_result: COPY atelier_senzori.db embeds the populated database into the image; combined with F-002, `sqlite3 atelier_senzori.db 'select * from users'` reveals all plaintext passwords from any copy of the image
findings.fix: Remove atelier_senzori.db from the COPY instruction. Initialize the database at container startup from environment-supplied credentials, never from a pre-seeded file committed to the image. If a seed is needed for demos, generate it with hashed passwords at first run.

findings.title: No rate limiting on /login enables unlimited brute-force
findings.intended_control: failed login attempts are bounded to prevent credential guessing
findings.crossed_boundary: attacker iterates passwords at network speed → account takeover
findings.observed_result: no counter, lockout, or delay between attempts; combined with F-002 and F-003 the attack is trivial

evidence.note: No Flask-Limiter, no attempt counter, no account lockout, no CAPTCHA.

findings.fix: Add Flask-Limiter (e.g., @limiter.limit("10/minute") on the login POST) or implement per-IP and per-username exponential backoff with a counter stored in the session or database.

findings.title: Backup script pseudonymizes usernames/locations but preserves plaintext passwords
findings.accepted_input: read access to a backup file produced by backup.sh
findings.intended_control: backup pseudonymization limits exposure of sensitive user data
findings.crossed_boundary: backup consumer → plaintext passwords for all users
findings.observed_result: backup.sh pseudonymizes users.username, senzori.cod, and senzori.locatie but does not alter the users.password column, which remains plaintext

evidence.note: UPDATE users SET username = ? — only username is replaced; password column untouched.

findings.fix: After pseudonymizing usernames, also overwrite the password column with a constant placeholder (e.g., UPDATE users SET password = 'REDACTED'). Note: this only matters if passwords are still stored as plaintext; applying F-002's fix first makes the hash non-reversible by design.

findings.title: Missing HTTP security response headers
findings.accepted_input: any HTTP response from the application
findings.intended_control: browser-enforced defences (CSP, frame-options, type-sniffing) limit attack surface
findings.crossed_boundary: absent headers weaken browser-side mitigations for XSS (F-001) and clickjacking
findings.affected_principal: users accessing the app via browser
findings.observed_result: Flask default responses carry no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, or Referrer-Policy headers

evidence.note: No after_request hook sets security headers; no Flask-Talisman or equivalent.

findings.fix: Add Flask-Talisman or an after_request hook that sets at minimum: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; X-Frame-Options: DENY; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; Referrer-Policy: same-origin.

findings.title: Demo credentials displayed to authenticated users on profile page
findings.accepted_input: GET /profil after logging in as alina or cosmin
findings.crossed_boundary: authenticated session → credential disclosure in page response
findings.observed_result: profile.html lines 17-21 render 'alina / alina123' or 'cosmin / cosmin123' in the authenticated page body
findings.fix: Remove the credential hints from the profile template. If demo instructions are needed, place them in a separate internal documentation page, not in the authenticated UI.

needs_validation.title: Session cookie missing Secure flag; cleartext session hijack depends on deployment
needs_validation.hypothesis: Flask's SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE defaults to False. If the app is accessed over HTTP (no TLS-terminating proxy), the signed session cookie is transmitted in cleartext, exposing it to network interception.

source_trace.note: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE not configured; Flask 3.1.3 default is False.

needs_validation.missing_fact: Whether a TLS-terminating reverse proxy is present in front of the app in all deployment environments.
needs_validation.validation_plan: Owner confirms: (1) Is HTTPS enforced at the proxy layer for all environments? (2) If not, add SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True to app.config and deploy behind HTTPS.

needs_validation.title: CSRF on /form POST — mitigated by Flask 3.1.3 SameSite=Lax default, but not explicitly configured
needs_validation.hypothesis: POST /form has no CSRF token. Flask 3.1.3 sets SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE='Lax' by default, which prevents cross-origin form submissions from carrying the session cookie in mainstream browsers. However, this is an implicit reliance on a framework default rather than an explicit defence.

source_trace.note: No CSRF token field in the form.

needs_validation.missing_fact: Explicit confirmation of Flask 3.1.3 SameSite=Lax default and no override in app config.
needs_validation.validation_plan: Owner confirms SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE is not overridden. For belt-and-suspenders: add Flask-WTF CSRF tokens or set SameSite=Strict explicitly in app config.
